inputs.notes: MODEL: component-built owner-FCF DCF, 10-year explicit horizon, per .claude/skills/dcf-methods/references/owner-fcf.md including the section 7 non-US/cyclical adaptations. Routed here because Skellerup is a straightforward profitable operating company (two-segment engineered polymer manufacturer) with a conservatively geared balance sheet -- none of the bank/REIT/LIC/holdco/distressed exclusions apply. Section 7 items applied: (a) WACC built from NZD inputs, not USD; (e) SBC-zero market -- SBC rows kept explicit at 0.0% and band_position set to null rather than a degenerate 0%; (f) risk charged ONCE, in the flows via probability-weighted scenarios, so the same 10.5% WACC is used in all three scenarios and no ad-hoc cyclicality premium is stacked on top. Leases: NZ IFRS 16 applies but Skellerup is an owner-occupier of its principal plants with immaterial lease liabilities and no separately disclosed lease principal; no lease adjustment made and lease_cost_pct is 0. No minority interests. NORMALISATION: FY2026 statutory NPAT of 67.7 includes a ~NZ$4.8m one-off Wigram fire insurance gain; all valuation anchors use NORMALISED NPAT 64.2 and NORMALISED EBIT 89.3. FY2026 is not from an annual report -- it is the 19-Aug-2026 results release, and the balance-sheet columns are absent by design. Working capital capture is NEGATIVE (-8% of the revenue change): this is an inventory- and receivables-heavy manufacturer, so growth ABSORBS cash rather than releasing it -- the opposite sign to a prepaid subscription business.

historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: MATERIAL AND CENTRAL TO THE VALUATION. Over ten years revenue compounded 6.32% but EBIT compounded 11.71% -- the entire 5.4pp wedge is margin expansion (EBIT margin 15.6% in FY2017 to 22.9% in FY2026), not volume. Margin expansion is finite and cannot be extrapolated, so the equity/revenue CAGRs (4.4-6.9%) rather than the EBIT/FCF CAGRs are the honest forward driver. Equity CAGR (5.41% 5yr) understates reinvestment economics because Skellerup pays out ~90% of earnings as dividends (30.0cps against 32.8cps EPS in FY2026), so book value barely grows -- this is a high-payout compounder, not a book-value compounder, which is why revenue CAGR and not equity CAGR was selected. FCF 3yr CAGR of 14.2% is flattered by a FY2023 starting point; the 5yr figure of 5.89% is the representative one.
historical_growth.notes: SBC is zero across the entire history, so the owner-FCF series equals the reported FCF series and adjusted and unadjusted CAGRs coincide. Interest income (<NZ$0.2m/yr) is immaterial but stripped for consistency.

scenario_narratives.base: Skellerup keeps its specification lock-in and its new-product cadence, but the ten-year run of record EBIT stops compounding at the top line's expense: revenue grows 6% in FY2027 (management is 'broadly comfortable' with consensus and reports steady early trading) and fades toward ~3% as the Fonterra 2026/27 payout cut to $9.25/kgMS works through farmer discretionary spend. The decisive assumption is margin. FY2026's 22.9% EBIT / 27.5% EBITDA margin is an all-time high reached after a 7.3pp expansion from FY2017's 15.6%; the base case fades EBITDA to a still-excellent 25.5% mid-cycle level rather than treating the peak as the new floor. Capex rises from 3.9% of revenue to ~4.6%, meeting D&A, because an asset-heavy manufacturer part-way through a modernisation and Wigram CV-line rebuild cannot under-invest against depreciation indefinitely.
scenario_narratives.bull: Management's stated 11-12% medium-term compound earnings ambition is delivered. Industrial's potable-water/wastewater exposure compounds against a structurally growing US infrastructure theme, the ~12.5% blended tariff regime stays 'substantially offset' permanently rather than temporarily, Agri holds its consumable replacement-cycle volumes through a softer payout, and the NZ$55m undrawn facility funds accretive bolt-on M&A. Margins do not merely hold at the record but creep to 28.5% EBITDA on mix and operating leverage. Revenue compounds 9% falling to 4.5%. Even this case reaches only $6.08 -- below the current price.
scenario_narratives.bear: The two external risks the company itself flags both bite. Fonterra's payout cut deepens and Agri's footwear and equipment-adjacent discretionary lines soften after a near-record season, while US tariff policy re-escalates against the ~37-40% of group revenue that is US-market exposed with ~85% of it manufactured in China, Vietnam and NZ -- a headwind management describes as 'substantially', not permanently, offset and subject to rates that 'change every week'. Revenue stalls at 1-1.5% for two years and EBITDA margin mean-reverts to 21.5%, roughly the FY2019-20 level, which is a return to normal rather than a crisis. Lumpy single-customer events like the H1 FY26 Health & Hygiene production pause recur.

wacc_rationale: 10.5% NZD-denominated, applied identically to all three scenarios. Built from NZD inputs per section 7(a): NZ 10-year government bond ~4.3% risk-free, equity risk premium ~6.0% (the standard NZ market premium; NZ equity premia run above US/AU on market depth), levered beta ~1.05 for a diversified industrial with a dairy-cyclical segment, giving ~10.6%, rounded to 10.5%. The balance sheet is effectively unlevered (net debt NZ$2.0m against a NZ$1.47bn market cap) so WACC and cost of equity coincide -- no debt-weighting benefit is taken. NO illiquidity premium is stacked: at a ~NZ$1.47bn market cap Skellerup is a mid-cap, not the micro-cap that would justify one. Per section 7(f), the genuine risk factors -- dairy-cycle exposure to the Fonterra payout cut, ~37-40% US-market revenue against fluid tariff policy, FX translation and raw-material/freight input costs -- are charged ONCE, in the bear-scenario flows and in the 25% bear weight, NOT a second time as a WACC premium. Using a higher WACC in the bear case than the bull would have charged the same risk a third time and was deliberately avoided.

entry_price.notes: Entry price = (PV of the ten interim owner-FCF years at 15% + terminal value computed at WACC then discounted back at 15% - net debt) / shares. Every scenario's 15% entry price sits far below the NZ$7.48 market price: even the bull case only clears a 15% hurdle if bought at NZ$4.50.

required_return_table.notes: At NZ$7.48 the base-case flows do not deliver even a 9% return; the price implies a required return below 6%.
required_return_table.note: Each row rebuilds the terminal value at that row's required return (min(Gordon@r, cap x FCF_N)), so the flows and the exit are charged the same rate. Corrected 2026-09-01.

sensitivity.notes: Base-case drivers flexed. Every one of the 25 cells sits below the NZ$7.48 market price; the highest, at an implausibly generous 8.5% WACC with 3.25% terminal growth, reaches NZ$5.60. Rows are flat at 8.5% WACC because the 15x terminal cap binds there -- correct behaviour for a cyclical.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: Shifted from the 15/50/35 house default to 25/50/25. Bear raised to 25% because two of the company's flagged downside risks are already in motion rather than hypothetical -- Fonterra's 2026/27 payout has been cut to $9.25/kgMS from ~$9.75, and management itself describes the tariff position as 'substantially' offset with rates that 'change every week' against 37-40% US-exposed revenue. Bull cut to 25% because that case needs several independent things to go right at once (margins hold at an all-time high AND tariffs stay neutralised permanently AND accretive M&A is executed AND Agri holds through a softer payout), which is exactly the situation the method file says should reduce bull weight. Base held at 50%: management's own repeated caution that 'these record results cannot continue ad infinitum' is the base case, in the company's own words.
probability_weighted.band_note: SBC is genuinely zero, so the house (SBC-expensed) and street (SBC-as-non-cash) bases are identical and the accounting-regime band collapses to a point. band_position is null per section 7(e), not a degenerate 0%.

sanity_check.basis: SBC is genuinely zero at Skellerup (verified against every cash flow statement FY2015-FY2026 and the EquityAwardTaxes kpi series, all 0), so the SBC-adjusted and unadjusted bases COINCIDE -- historical and implied multiples are computed on the same basis and the house/street band collapses to a point. Historical multiples use the JUNE fiscal-year-end monthly close from the Yahoo 10y series against the FY rows of SKL.NZ_Metrics.csv. Earnings are NORMALISED: FY2026 uses NPAT 64.2 (excluding the NZ$4.8m Wigram insurance gain) and FY2024 uses 50.014 (excluding the 3.121 abnormal tax item).

reverse_dcf.growth_implied_by_price: 11.1% revenue CAGR for ten years if the record 27.5% EBITDA margin is held flat forever
reverse_dcf.detail: Holding the base-case mid-cycle drivers, NZ$7.48 requires a ~6.0% discount rate -- below the NZ 10-year government bond plus any equity premium, i.e. a negative risk premium. Alternatively, holding the all-time-high margin flat in perpetuity and using the house 10.5% WACC, the price requires 11.1% annual revenue growth for a decade against a 6.32% ten-year actual. Neither is a defensible base case. Even at an 8.0% WACC with a 20x terminal cap the base drivers give only NZ$6.40.

sanity_check.diagnosis: No trip in either direction. The base IV of NZ$4.43 is 40.7% BELOW the NZ$7.48 market price, and the trip conditions guard against DCF over-valuation, so none fires. The material question was the reverse -- whether the model is unfairly harsh -- and it survives that test too: the base IV implies 13.5x normalised P/E and 8.1x EV/EBITDA, which are below but within reach of SKL's own ex-outlier history (16.75x and 9.63x), whereas the market at 22.8x P/E and 13.7x EV/EBITDA is above every non-melt-up year in the decade and matches only the FY2021-22 bubble that subsequently de-rated 21%. The gap is not a modelling artefact but a single explicit judgment: the base case fades EBITDA margin from the all-time-high 27.5% to a mid-cycle 25.5%, because the ten-year 11.71% EBIT CAGR was produced by 7.3pp of margin expansion on only 6.32% revenue growth, and margin expansion is arithmetically finite. If the peak margin is instead permanent AND revenue compounds at 9%, the bull case still only reaches NZ$6.08 -- 19% below the current price. The market is paying for a continuation of margin expansion that the company's own management declines to promise ('these record results cannot continue ad infinitum').

valuation_philosophy.summary: Skellerup is a genuinely high-quality business trading at a price that already pays for its quality and then some. The verdict is OVERVALUED at NZ$7.48, on a weighted IV of NZ$4.51 -- and the reason is arithmetic, not pessimism about the company.
valuation_philosophy.the_central_judgment: Over the ten years to FY2026 revenue compounded 6.32% while EBIT compounded 11.71%. The entire 5.4pp wedge is margin expansion: EBIT margin went from 15.6% in FY2017 to 22.9% in FY2026, an all-time high, in the tenth consecutive record year. That expansion was real and well-earned -- specification lock-in, new-product cadence, disciplined cost control -- but it is finite in a way revenue growth is not. A valuation that projects the 11.7% earnings CAGR forward is implicitly assuming margins keep expanding forever. This model instead grows revenue at a defensible 6% fading to 3% and fades EBITDA margin from 27.5% to a still-excellent 25.5% mid-cycle level. That single decision is most of the gap to market.
valuation_philosophy.what_the_price_requires: A reverse DCF is unusually stark here. At the base drivers, NZ$7.48 implies a ~6.0% discount rate -- a negative equity risk premium against the ~4.3% NZ 10-year bond. Alternatively, holding the record margin flat forever at a 10.5% WACC, it implies 11.1% revenue growth for a decade against 6.32% actual. The bull case -- margins creeping to 28.5%, revenue at 9%, tariffs permanently neutralised, accretive M&A executed -- reaches only NZ$6.08, still 19% below the price. When the optimistic case does not reach the market price, the market is not pricing an optimistic case; it is pricing a better one than the business has ever delivered.
valuation_philosophy.why_not_manufacture_upside: The prompt's specific warning was a base-case multi-bagger while the price sits at the top of its 10-year range. The honest result went the other way, and the temptation to close a 41% gap by nudging WACC to 8% and the terminal cap to 20x was tested explicitly: it produces NZ$6.40, still below the price. There is no defensible combination of NZD-built discount rate and mid-cycle margin that reaches NZ$7.48. Rather than reach for one, the model reports the gap and names the one assumption -- permanence of a peak margin -- on which a bull would have to disagree.
valuation_philosophy.quality_is_not_in_dispute: Nothing here says avoid the company. Net debt is NZ$2.0m against a NZ$55m facility; operating cash flow of NZ$83.6m covers a 30.0cps dividend comfortably; Agri's consumable replacement cycle is genuinely defensive and Industrial's water/wastewater exposure is a real structural theme; management has neutralised a serious tariff shock inside a year. The FY2026 cash flow also passes the quality test the method file demands -- OCF of 83.6 is almost exactly normalised NPAT plus D&A (82.2), so there is no working-capital windfall inflating the base, unlike the deferred-revenue traps this engine was built to catch. The issue is entirely price. The 15% hurdle entry price is NZ$3.38 weighted; a patient buyer's opportunity is a de-rating, not a downgrade.
valuation_philosophy.what_would_change_this: Evidence that the 22.9% EBIT margin is structural rather than cyclical -- two or three more years holding it through a soft dairy payout, or a mix shift into higher-margin Industrial water products large enough to reset the group average. A step-change in revenue growth from bolt-on M&A deployed off the unlevered balance sheet would also move the base case, since the model currently credits none. Conversely a Fonterra payout below $9.00/kgMS or a tariff re-escalation on the 37-40% US-exposed revenue would move weight toward the bear case.
